questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: What Makes a Stage a Stage
questions.learningObjective: state what qualifies a period of development as a stage
questions.stem: A proposed stage begins when the form of a child's thinking changes, holds for a few years, and is then replaced by another such change. What is doing the defining work?

options.text: A change in the form of thinking, since each stage sets up the next rather than just adding more
A fixed age of onset, because a stage is defined by the calendar date every child reaches it
options.misconception: believes a stage is fixed by an age rather than by a change in kind

options.text: A rise in the number of items a child can manage, because capacity is what separates them
options.misconception: confuses a stage with a bigger quantity of the same ability

options.text: An increase in the rate of improvement, because learning faster marks the start of a stage
options.misconception: reads a change in speed of gain as a change in the form of thought

questions.explanation: A stage in the strict sense is a period marked by a change in kind rather than amount, so the way a child solves problems is structured differently, and the later structure is built on the earlier one. That is why the count of items handled and the speed of improvement are not what define the boundaries, since both can move without anything having been reorganised. The tempting belief that a fixed age defines a stage fails because onset varies widely between children while the change in form still occurs. The belief about capacity fails because more of the same performance is a continuous gain, not a new structure. The belief about rate fails for the same reason in a different quantity, since going faster at the same kind of thinking leaves the structure alone.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change is in how much or in how the problem is being thought about.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Continuous and Discontinuous Change
questions.learningObjective: distinguish continuous from discontinuous accounts of a developmental change
questions.stem: One account of language holds that a child's first words are fewer, shorter and less accurate than an adult's, without being different in kind. What is it claiming?

options.text: Change is continuous, because the childhood form differs from the adult one only in amount and accuracy
Change is discontinuous, because a smaller word is a qualitatively earlier form of word than an adult one
options.misconception: reads a difference of quantity as a difference of underlying kind

options.text: Change is continuous, because children and adults learn words by entirely different processes
options.misconception: claims a change of process in support of an account of smooth change

options.text: Change is discontinuous, because a child saying fewer words has a smaller underlying capacity
options.misconception: tries to make a quantity gap into a separate earlier stage

questions.explanation: The claim being made is that the early and the mature form sit on one continuum, so a child's first words are the adult's words at a lower point rather than a different kind of thing. A continuous account predicts a smooth gradient with no structural break, and that is exactly what the description of smaller and less accurate words describes. The tempting belief that this is a discontinuous claim fails because no change of kind is asserted anywhere in the description. The belief that a change of learning process supports continuity fails because a different process would normally be taken to mean a different structure, and the description says nothing about processes. The claim about a smaller underlying capacity fails because a reduction in quantity is what the account is explicitly denying.
questions.hint: Ask whether the childhood form is described as a different thing or a smaller amount of the same one.

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: What a Maturation Explanation Claims
questions.learningObjective: state what a maturation explanation does and does not claim
questions.stem: A six-year-old does a puzzle an adult finds hard, and the puzzle needs no reading. Which statement is the maturational explanation?

options.text: The underlying capacity is there and unfolds with time, given surroundings that do not block it
The capacity is entirely absent until maturation finishes, and nothing in the meantime could matter
options.misconception: adds a claim of complete insulation from the environment

options.text: The capacity is present and already fully acquired, so the difficulty must be a shortage of practice
options.misconception: converts a maturational account into a claim about a learned skill

options.text: The capacity is a skill that has to be learned, and puzzle work is the input that installs it
options.misconception: describes a learned skill rather than an unfolding capacity

questions.explanation: A maturation explanation says the capacity is already present in rudimentary form and that it is the child's own development, rather than training, that brings it to full working order, which is why the account is offered for a capacity that appears without being taught. The qualification matters: maturation means unfolding, not immunity, so the account still requires that the environment not obstruct the development, and an account claiming the environment could not matter at all would be a stronger and less defensible claim than the one usually made. The tempting belief about complete absence fails because a capacity that is not there cannot unfold. The belief about practice fails because it describes a skill acquired by doing, which is the opposite of what the account is for. The last option states the learning explanation rather than the maturational one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the account is about something unfolding or something being installed by practice.

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Critical and Sensitive Periods
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a critical period from a sensitive one by the shape of its effects
questions.stem: For one skill, an experience in its window leaves adults normal, one slightly outside leaves them partly impaired, and one far outside leaves them much worse. Which label fits?

A critical period, because the experience can only be had inside the window and never at any other time
options.misconception: labels a graded effect as though the window admitted of no substitute

options.text: A sensitive period, because the effect is all or nothing at the window's edge and never graded
options.misconception: describes an abrupt boundary as though effects were graded

options.text: A critical period, because anything outside the window leaves performance entirely normal
options.misconception: claims no effect at all outside the window where one is reported

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: The Pattern That Marks Attachment
questions.learningObjective: identify proximity seeking with a particular caregiver as the pattern of attachment
questions.stem: A toddler explores a room, looks back to where an adult sits, and settles fastest when that particular adult comes back. What does that show?

options.text: A particular caregiver is being used as a source of safety that the child checks and returns to
The adult is being approached for material things, since returning is how the child gets given things
options.misconception: reduces proximity seeking to an instrumental reward arrangement

options.text: The child is following a route it is required to take, since returning is the only way out of the room
options.misconception: explains the return as a physical constraint on movement

options.text: The child is copying the adult's walk, so the return is an imitated movement and nothing more
options.misconception: reads a seeking pattern as a single copied motor act

The belief about a required route fails because a toddler is not confined by the room. The imitation claim fails because a copied walk does not explain the speed of recovery, which is a function of who the adult is.

questions.stem: A caregiver is consistently responsive for a year, and the child afterwards expects other people to be dependable and looks for that in new ones. What is that?

A temperament, a stable behavioural disposition that is present from the first weeks of an infant's life
options.misconception: confuses an expectation built from relationships with an early disposition

options.text: A moral stage, a set of principles about fairness that the child can already state in words
options.misconception: mistakes an expectation about people for a reasoned principle about fairness

options.misconception: treats a general expectation as a store of specific dated episodes

The episodic-memory claim fails because the child is generalising rather than replaying, and a specific memory would not tell the child what to expect from a stranger.

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: What a Temperament Classification Measures
questions.learningObjective: identify the dimensions of a temperament classification
questions.stem: A researcher rates infants on activity, strength of reaction, approach to people and readiness to startle. What kind of classification is being built?

options.misconception: treats a disposition as a stage in a sequence of thought forms

options.misconception: imposes an ordering on independent dimensions that do not have one

questions.learningObjective: explain goodness of fit as a match between a child's temperament and a caregiver's

options.misconception: turns a mismatch of dispositions into an absence of any relationship

options.misconception: jumps from an interactional strain to a delay in physical development

options.misconception: confuses attributing agency to a thing with attributing it to people

questions.learningObjective: identify a task outside the reach of reasoning about objects present

options.misconception: claims conservation is lost once a harder quantity question is asked

options.misconception: treats a concrete achievement as evidence of the next stage of reasoning

options.text: Reasoning about other children, since anticipating a class's answer goes beyond concrete thought

The claim about other children fails because nothing in the question involves predicting anyone else.

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: What a Correlation Coefficient Cannot Show
questions.learningObjective: identify the claim a correlation coefficient does not license
questions.stem: Across forty schools, hours of revision correlate with scores at 0.6. Which claim does that coefficient not support on its own?

options.text: That more revision goes with higher scores, and not which of the two produces the other

options.misconception: treats a real association as though it settled a direction of cause

options.text: That the association is a moderate one, since 0.6 sits between small and very strong
options.misconception: reads a moderate correlation as though it identified a causal direction

options.text: That the two measures are related in this sample, since the association is not near zero
options.misconception: concludes that a coefficient determines which variable acted on the other

The claim about moderateness fails because the size of the association is a description and not a licence to infer a mechanism. The final claim fails because relatedness and direction are exactly what a correlation cannot separate.
questions.hint: Ask what the number describes about the two measures, and what it is silent about.

questions.stem: Half the patients in a trial get a new drink and half get a similar-tasting placebo, and both groups are told the drink is under test without being told which they received. What does that arrangement address?

questions.learningObjective: state what randomisation protects against and what it does not promise
questions.stem: Two hundred patients are allocated at random to a new drug or to the standard one, and the halves turn out similar in age, severity and prior treatment. What has the randomisation bought?

options.text: A good chance that known participant differences did not land in one arm of the study
A guarantee that the drug's effect will be large enough for the study to be able to detect it

options.text: A guarantee that the patients will take the drug consistently enough for the result to count
options.misconception: treats allocation as though it controlled what participants did afterwards

options.text: A guarantee that the number of patients is enough for the difference found to be real
options.misconception: claims randomisation settles sample size and statistical adequacy

The consistency claim fails because adherence is a decision made after allocation. The sample-size claim fails because two hundred patients is a separate decision about power and nothing about the lottery of allocation changes it.

questions.learningObjective: identify what a cross-sectional comparison leaves unresolved

questions.learningObjective: read a fall after selecting on an extreme score as regression to the mean
questions.stem: A service accepts only children scoring in the top tenth on a reading check. Re-tested two months later with no instruction given, the group's mean has fallen to the fiftieth percentile. Why?

options.text: Selecting on an extreme score selects error as well as ability, and the error is not repeated
Reading improves once a child is referred, so the fall from the ninetieth to the fiftieth is a gain
options.misconception: reads a fall against the group as progress towards a typical score

options.text: The second check is a harder instrument, so every child scores lower on it than on the first
options.misconception: explains the fall as a property of the measure rather than of selection

options.text: The children who fell furthest are the ones who gained most from being referred
options.misconception: assumes the largest falls mark the largest treatment gains

questions.explanation: Taking the top tenth means taking children whose scores were high partly because the measurement flattered them that day, and on a second occasion that flattery is not repeated, so the group converges towards its own ordinary level with no instruction of any kind. The harder-instrument claim fails because a change in the measure would shift every child, and nothing reports that other children were also tested. The largest-gain claim fails because it presumes an intervention whose absence is stated, and it also inverts the logic, since the biggest falls would then be the biggest effects.

options.misconception: blames the self-report measure and ignores the selection that produced it

options.misconception: rejects a plausible proportion on numerical grounds alone

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: The Step That Decides Whether Stress Does Harm
questions.learningObjective: explain appraisal as the point at which a demand becomes a threat or a challenge
questions.stem: Two staff face the same deadline, and one is ill afterwards while the other is not. Explain where appraisal sits in that sequence and what it predicts.

answer.exemplar: The event itself is identical in the two cases, so whatever differs has to be inserted between the demand and the response rather than being a property of the demand. That is the appraisal, the sense a person forms of what the demand means for them, and two people can read the same deadline as a threat they are not equipped to meet and as a challenge they can work through. The consequences claimed for that step run in both directions: a demand read as an unpredictable threat with no way of coping is what sets off a prolonged response, and where a person judges coping to be available the response is shorter and the sense of being worn down is smaller. Coping is the second half of the story, and it enters after the appraisal rather than in place of it, since an intention to cope does not help if the demand has already been read as hopeless. A response worth noting is that the deadline alone cannot explain the outcome, so any account that stops at the amount of work would predict both people should fare alike. What would support the appraisal account is a measure taken before the deadline that shows the two people differing in expected coping, with the illness following that difference rather than the workload; what would weaken it is illness following the heavier workload irrespective of what either person expected.

questions.explanation: The answer has to place appraisal before the physiological and health consequences, explain why the two staff differ despite an identical demand, and say what would count as evidence either way.
questions.hint: Ask what the two people did differently, given that nothing about the deadline itself was different.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Why an Intention So Often Stops Short of an Act
questions.learningObjective: explain the gap between stated intention and performed behaviour
questions.stem: Most people surveyed say they will exercise weekly and far fewer are found doing so. Explain why the gap is large, and say what a survey figure can and cannot tell you.

answer.exemplar: The two figures come from different moments and the gap between them is not a sign that people are lying. An intention is formed when the question is asked, and at that point the costs of acting are usually remote or abstract while the benefits can be imagined vividly, which makes the plan easy to endorse. The costs then arrive at the moment of acting, when they are immediate, concrete and paid for in time, effort or discomfort, and at that moment the balance tips the other way. The size of the gap is therefore a property of the gap between imagining and doing, and it widens for intentions whose cost is deferred and whose benefit is delayed, which is why health-related intentions are particularly prone to it. A survey figure can report what people endorse when asked and is useful for that purpose, since agreement still varies meaningfully between groups. It cannot report what any given person will do, and using it to estimate rates of behaviour overstates them, often by a large margin. The designs that close the gap are the ones that measure the act: records, observation and follow-up, where the thing being counted is the behaviour and not the endorsement. That distinction is why a programme judged only on intentions may report excellent results while behaviour is unchanged.

questions.explanation: The answer has to explain the timing of costs and benefits rather than accusing respondents of dishonesty, and to state what an intention measure is and is not able to report.
questions.hint: Ask when the costs of acting are felt, and at what moment the balance between cost and benefit is settled.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Following Children Forward and Comparing Them Sideways
questions.learningObjective: explain what a longitudinal design resolves and what it still cannot establish
questions.stem: A handbook reports a sharp rise in reasoning between six and nine, taken from different children at each age. Explain what following the same children would and would not settle.

answer.exemplar: Two explanations fit the handbook figure equally well. The children's reasoning may have improved as they got older, or six-year-olds and nine-year-olds may simply be different sorts of person, with the older group differing in schooling, language or home in ways that also show up in how they reason. Comparing different people at each age cannot separate those, because the comparison is built out of two samples rather than out of one sample followed over time. Following the same children makes it a comparison of two states of one sample, and a difference between age groups that was really a difference between samples will not reproduce. That much is settled by the design. What the design does not settle is the cause of any change it does record, because there is no comparison group and nothing was manipulated: children may improve because of maturation, teaching, practice or a combination, and a single group followed forward cannot distinguish those. It also has costs, since the same children are followed over years, some drop out, and the ones who remain may differ from the ones who left, so attrition becomes a rival explanation for any late change. A useful addition is to run a parallel cohort measured only once at nine, which gives a same-age comparison and a check on whether the followed sample still resembles other nine-year-olds. The handbook claim would then be supported if the within-person rise appeared and the cohort control behaved like the followed children, and weakened if the rise vanished or if the two nine-year-old groups diverged.

questions.explanation: The answer has to name the two explanations the cross-sectional figure leaves open, say what following the same children resolves, and be explicit that dating a change is not explaining it.
questions.hint: Ask whether a difference between two age groups could be a difference between two kinds of person instead of a change in one person.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Why Watching a Model Changes What a Person Does
questions.learningObjective: explain the belief about capability that model-watching is meant to change
questions.stem: Patients who watch others in their own position managing difficult days afterwards report coping more often. Explain what the watching is meant to change.

answer.exemplar: The programme is aimed at a belief about capability rather than at knowledge or at desire, and that is what a model supplies. Someone who has not done a thing may hold two separate doubts about it: whether it is worth doing and whether they could manage it. Watching a similar person manage it addresses the second doubt, because the demonstration shows both that the situation can be handled and that a person much like the viewer handled it, and the second half is the part a demonstration of an exceptional person would not supply. That is why the matching of the model to the viewer is a design requirement rather than a convenience, and why such programmes often pair the models with opportunities to act and record progress, since a belief of this kind is built from one's own successes more readily than from watching others'. The claim is not that the patient has been given information, because information about the condition is not what the models carry, nor that the patient now wants the outcome more, because wanting is untouched by watching conduct. What would support the account is a measure of the capability belief taken before and after, with the change in reported coping following it, and a comparison condition given information or encouragement without a model. What would weaken it is coping that increases where no such belief changed, since a rise in the act without a rise in the belief would suggest something other than capability was doing the work.

questions.explanation: The answer has to identify the specific belief being targeted, explain why the model is matched to the viewer, and give the evidence that would support or weaken that reading.
questions.hint: Ask which of two doubts about a course of action a demonstration can remove, and which it cannot.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about temperament as a predictor of later outcomes
questions.stem: Four claims about temperament are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: Temperament is a disposition about behaviour that is measurable before anything is learnt is claimed
options.misconception: concedes a disposition while ignoring that infants are already learning

options.text: Temperament can predict a later outcome without being the only thing that predicts it
A temperament trait fixes an outcome, so a child rated high cannot end up low on it
options.misconception: treats an early disposition as a fixed destination

options.text: A trait measured in the parents also predicts that outcome, making it a second line of evidence

questions.explanation: Two claims are safe here and two overreach. Being a valid predictor is not being a complete explanation, so the first of the supported pair commits only to a tendency that holds across a long stretch of life, which is a modest and well-supported claim. The second supported claim is that a trait measured in the parents predicts the same outcome, so the account has a second line of evidence rather than a single measure, and a study that reported only the child's own rating would be leaving out part of what it found. The tempting first option fails because infancy is a period of constant learning, so a disposition described as measurable before anything is learnt is describing when the measure was taken rather than a sealed state. The fixed-destination option fails because a disposition is a tendency rather than a verdict, and tendencies are modulated by experience, so a rating predicts an outcome without deciding it. Where the same trait shows up in parents and children, inherited and modelled routes both remain open and the data cannot separate them.
questions.hint: Ask what being a predictor commits a claim to, and whether the two ratings are the same measure.

options.text: Illness has no bearing on stress, since a third factor would be needed to explain the link

Both of those statements are about what the data permit, and neither adds a mechanism that was not there. The tempting causal claim fails because measuring two things across the same year is a property of the calendar and not of the relationship, and it would fail just as thoroughly if both had been measured in different years. The final claim fails because raising an alternative explanation is not a reason to deny the association, and the two moves are independent: a third factor could explain a link that is nonetheless plainly present in the data.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Weaknesses in a Before and After Study
questions.learningObjective: identify the design faults that block a causal reading of a comparison
questions.stem: A clinic compares patients' scores before and after a programme. Which two faults would most damage what it can claim? Select both.

options.text: No control group, so ordinary improvement over time cannot be separated from the programme
Only high scorers were enrolled, so later scores are expected to fall for reasons of selection
The scores were taken in the same room each time, so the conditions were kept constant
options.misconception: mistakes a sensible control for a threat to the conclusion

options.text: The scores were recorded by a member of staff, so all such records are unreliable
options.misconception: dismisses an entire class of measurement because one recorder was involved

questions.explanation: Both of the selected faults attack the comparison itself rather than the reliability of the numbers. Without a control group the study cannot tell a programme effect from the ordinary course of events, since scores often improve on a second sitting for reasons having nothing to do with the programme, and enrolling only high scorers adds a second problem in which the group is expected to drift downwards for reasons that have nothing to do with the programme either. The tempting third claim fails because holding the room constant is a precaution that improves comparability, and there is no sense in which it weakens the conclusion. The fourth claim fails because a staff recorder is a routine arrangement found in most studies, and the appropriate response would be to blind the scorer to the time point rather than to abandon the measurement.
questions.hint: Ask which faults change what the comparison can mean, rather than which choices were sensible.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: The Components of a Health Belief
questions.learningObjective: map interview and leaflet material onto the components of a health-belief account
questions.stem: A nurse asks how likely a patient feels a complication is, how serious it would be if it came, and what the treatment involves. Which two questions are well chosen? Select both.

options.text: How likely the complication is, which is the question about personal susceptibility
How serious it would be, which is the question about the consequences of harm
What the treatment involves, which measures the barrier the patient must get past
options.misconception: reads a description of the treatment as a barrier to taking it

options.text: How long the consultation is, which measures the time the patient must give up
options.misconception: treats consultation length as the barrier the account is about

questions.explanation: The account turns on two judgments about harm that can be asked directly: how likely the harm is for this person, and how bad it would be if it arrived, and those are the two questions that map onto the components without reinterpretation. The two rejected items describe what the treatment and the appointment involve, which are facts rather than judgments, and asking for a description of them does not measure whether the patient sees a difficulty. The tempting third claim fails because a description of the treatment is content, while a barrier is the patient's own estimate of what would make acting hard, such as the cost, the effort or the fear. The fourth claim fails on the same ground, and consultation length is at most one candidate barrier rather than the component itself, since the patient may not regard time as a difficulty at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether each item is a judgment the patient makes or a fact the nurse supplies.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: How a Stated Intention Comes to Nothing
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a plan fails to become an act
questions.stem: A weekly exercise plan is endorsed in a survey and then never carried out. Put these five events in the order that leads from the endorsement to nothing happening.

options.text: A person forms an intention to act weekly and endorses it when asked
At the moment of asking, the costs of acting are distant and the benefits easy to imagine
At the moment of acting, the costs are immediate and the benefits still some way off
The cost outweighs the benefit at that moment and the act is put off once more
The postponement repeats until the plan stops being carried out at all

questions.explanation: The sequence begins with the intention being endorsed, and the second step is what makes that endorsement easy: while the act is still hypothetical its costs are remote and its benefits vivid, so the balance is settled in favour of acting before anyone has had to pay anything. The third step is the one that undoes it, because at the moment of acting the two sides of the balance have swapped places, and the fourth and fifth steps are the repetition that turns one missed week into a broken habit. Nothing here requires dishonesty, and the same person can endorse the plan sincerely at every survey. The wrong order that places the immediate costs before the endorsement fails because the postponement is caused by the reversal of the balance, and the reversal cannot precede the plan. The wrong order that places the repetition before the decision to put the act off fails because each postponement is a fresh decision, made after the costs are felt.
questions.hint: Start with the endorsement, then track what changes about the costs between asking and acting.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: The Sequence of a Randomised Trial
questions.learningObjective: order the steps from allocation to a conclusion about effect
questions.stem: A clinic runs a trial of a new treatment against a comparison condition. Put these five events in the order in which the trial moves from allocation to a conclusion.

options.text: Patients are allocated at random to the treatment or to the comparison condition
Each patient is given whatever their allocation assigned them, without being told which
The outcome is measured in both conditions on the same schedule and instrument
The two conditions are compared on that outcome, and any difference is estimated
The estimate is judged against what chance alone would produce in a comparison this size

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by what each step requires the previous one to have supplied, and allocation has to come first because every later comparison rests on the two groups having been formed without regard to the outcome. Delivery comes next, and withholding the information about which condition a patient is in is part of that step because it prevents expectations from differing between the two arms. Measurement has to follow in both conditions on one schedule and one instrument, since a difference between conditions in how the outcome was obtained would be indistinguishable from a difference in the outcome itself. The comparison and then the judgement against chance are the last two steps, and the second of them is the one that stops a study reporting a difference it should expect to see by luck. The wrong order that measures before delivering fails because there would be nothing to measure the effect of. The wrong order that concludes before the comparison fails because an estimate is what the comparison produces.
questions.hint: Start with the step that makes the two groups comparable, and end with the step that decides whether the difference is meaningful.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: From a Demanding Event to a Health Outcome
questions.learningObjective: order the claimed chain from a demand through appraisal to illness
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which the account of stress and illness has them occurring.

options.text: A demand arrives that has to be met within a fixed time and with limited control
The demand is appraised as something the person cannot cope with or control
A response is set off that is intended to be sustained while the demand continues
The person copes with part of the demand and the response stays switched on for the rest
Wear on the body accumulates until illness or a slowdown in performance appears

questions.explanation: Nothing can follow the demand until it has been appraised, because the same demand read as manageable and as hopeless produces different accounts of what happens next, and that is why two people with identical work can end differently. The sustained response follows the appraisal rather than the demand, since the response is a reaction to what the demand means rather than to its size. Coping comes after the response is under way, and the two interact rather than standing in a queue, because coping is what determines how long the response stays switched on. The health outcome is last because it is the accumulated result of a response that was not brought down. The wrong order that puts coping before appraisal fails because whether coping will be attempted depends on the reading of the demand, which is the earlier step. The wrong order that puts the outcome before the coping fails because the outcome is claimed to follow from a response sustained by coping that did not work.
questions.hint: Start with what arrives, then insert the judgment of it before anything physical can follow.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Cohort Size After Losses
questions.learningObjective: compute how many participants remain after a stated loss from a cohort
questions.stem: A study follows a cohort of 500 people for ten years and loses contact with 15 percent of them. How many people are still being followed?
questions.explanation: The share remaining is 100 percent minus 15 percent, which is 85 percent, and 85 percent of 500 is 0.85 times 500, giving 425. The figure is worth computing because a loss of this size does more than shrink the sample, since the people who drop out tend to differ from those who stay and so a shrinking group changes in composition as well as in size.
questions.hint: Take the complement of the loss, then multiply it by the starting cohort.

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: How Many Act on an Offer
questions.learningObjective: apply a conversion rate to an expressed intention to get a head count
questions.stem: Of 200 people offered a place on a health programme, 70 percent say they will take it, and 40 percent of those who said so actually enrol. How many enrol?
questions.explanation: Seventy percent of 200 is 140 people who say they will take it, and 40 percent of 140 is 0.4 times 140, which is 56 who enrol. The same figure can be reached in one step as 200 multiplied by 0.7 multiplied by 0.4, and the gap between 140 and 56 is the practical size of the intention gap for this programme.
questions.hint: Work out how many say yes first, then apply the second rate to that smaller group.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Extra Errors After a Week of Short Sleep
questions.learningObjective: compute an added error rate per hundred between two sleep conditions
questions.stem: On a signal task, 18 of 200 responses after a week of five hours' sleep a night are wrong, against 8 of 200 after a week of nine. How many more wrong responses per hundred is that?
questions.explanation: The two rates are 18 out of 200, which is 9 percent, and 8 out of 200, which is 4 percent, and the difference between them is 9 minus 4, which is 5 percentage points, or 5 extra wrong responses in every hundred. Because the two groups are the same size the counts can be read straight as percentages, which is the check on the working.
questions.hint: Turn both counts into percentages out of two hundred, then subtract the smaller from the larger.
